newsitem.title: FRANCE: French rail unions raise spectre of Oct 17 strike.
newsitem.headline: French rail unions raise spectre of Oct 17 strike.

text.p: The two most powerful unions in France's SNCF state railways have raised the spectre of a strike along with civil service unions on October 17 after a meeting between a rail staff committee and SNCF management.

The Communist-led CGT union said after the meeting on Tuesday that it was proposing talks among rail workers and other unions on the possibility of a "day of action" on October 17 amid concern over staff cuts and other worries about the SNCF's future.

Rail workers spearheaded a crippling 24-day strike and wider unrest late last year when the centre-right government of Prime Minister Alain Juppe proposed ending their early pension rights -- proposals which have since been scrapped.

The gripe this time, over programmed cuts in staffing levels and a modernisation plan which involves taking huge debts off the SNCF's hands, is harder to measure in terms of its potential to mobilise the railworkers themselves or wider public support.

Bruno Dalberto of the Socialist CFDT union told Reuters after the meeting on Tuesday that his union would decide after further internal talks on Wednesday whether to join a day of action on October 17, and could well do so.

Dalberto, whose union has opposed a reform and debt relief plan for the SNCF since it was unveiled in June, said a one-day strike at the same time as civil service unions had always been on the cards as far as his union was concerned.
"We had already said it was probable that we'd join the others in the civil service on October 17," Dalberto said.

A statement from the CGT union, the biggest union within the railways, highlighted that the staff committee which met SNCF chairman Louis Gallois, had voted overwhelmingly against the modernisation plan for the SNCF "in its current form".
It said 16 staff representatives from the CGT, CFDT and the smaller CFTC unions had voted against the modernisation plan, with two abstensions and just two in favour.

That plan commits the government to take 125 billion French francs ($24.40 billion) of debt off the loss-making SNCF's hands by spinning it off into another state company which would also become owner of the track and other infrastructure.

The CFDT is opposed to this on the ground that the split paves the way for privatisation if political imperatives change in the future, while the CGT also noted that staff levels were set to shrink by another 4,900 this year.
Staff levels fell by about the same number in 1995, to about 180,000.
There are also union fears that the modernisation plan does not commit the government firmly enough in legal terms.

A rail strike on October 17 would coincide with a strike called by seven unions in the civil service to protest against plans to cut the civil service by 6,000 next year. The unions are also demanding the opening of pay negotiations.
Teachers have set a 24-hour strike on the same issues for next Monday. ($1=5.124 French Franc)
